body:
How a trading company became a government

The English East India Company was established as a trading company under a royal charter granted in 1600. Its original purpose was commerce, not the administration of Indian territories. As the Company acquired political and military power, however, it needed officials to collect revenue, maintain order, settle disputes and enforce its decisions.

The Battle of Plassey in 1757 strengthened the Company's political position in Bengal. Its victory at the Battle of Buxar in 1764 further consolidated that position. In 1765, Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II granted the Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.

Meaning of Diwani

Diwani was the authority to administer and collect land revenue and other revenue. It gave the Company a major source of income and made financial administration an essential part of its territorial rule.

Revenue collection required more than demanding taxes. The Company had to maintain records of landholders, villages and payments; appoint officials; and establish procedures for disputes. The administration therefore expanded from commercial offices into a system of territorial government.

Presidencies and districts

The Company's principal administrative centres were the Bengal, Bombay and Madras Presidencies. A presidency was a large territorial and administrative division governed through its own governor and council. These divisions developed at different times and did not initially have identical powers or institutions.

As British authority expanded, the district became an important unit of local administration. A district officer dealt with revenue and, depending on the period and province, also exercised or coordinated executive and magisterial responsibilities. Courts and police establishments operated alongside the revenue administration.

Company rule, parliamentary control and Crown rule

Three authorities must be distinguished. The East India Company directly administered its territories during Company rule. The British Parliament increasingly regulated the Company through legislation, beginning with the Regulating Act of 1773. The British Crown assumed direct responsibility for governing British India in 1858.

Company administration did not mean that every Indian kingdom was governed directly by a British collector. Some territories remained under Indian rulers who entered into political arrangements with the British. Directly administered British districts and princely states therefore had different administrative positions.

The original royal charter of 1600 established the Company's trading privileges. The later Charter Acts of 1793, 1813, 1833 and 1853 were parliamentary measures that renewed or altered its privileges and governing powers. They should not be confused with the founding charter.

Prelims focus

  • 1600: royal charter establishing the English East India Company.
  • 1757: Battle of Plassey.
  • 1764: Battle of Buxar.
  • 1765: Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa granted to the Company.
  • The 3 principal Company Presidencies were Bengal, Bombay and Madras.
  • Trap: Parliamentary regulation began before direct Crown rule commenced in 1858.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 2, From Trade to Territory, printed pp. 9–15 and 21–22, 2020–21 printing; UK Parliament, East India Company and Raj 1785–1858, sections on Company government and the end of Company rule, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Revenue collection and record-keeping became central functions of Company administration.

title: From Trading Company to Colonial Government

body:
Why Parliament began regulating the Company

As the East India Company acquired territories and revenue, its decisions affected people far beyond its shareholders and merchants. Complaints about its administration and financial difficulties encouraged the British Parliament to exercise greater supervision. The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first major parliamentary step towards controlling the Company's government in India.

Regulating Act of 1773

The Act strengthened the position of Bengal within the Company's administration. It changed the Governor of Bengal into the Governor-General of Bengal and provided an executive council of 4 members to assist him. Warren Hastings became the first Governor-General of Bengal.

The Governor-General in Council acquired supervisory authority over the Bombay and Madras Presidencies, particularly in important political and military matters. This was an early step towards centralisation: decisions affecting more than one Presidency were increasingly brought under the Bengal government rather than left entirely to separate Presidency authorities.

The Act also authorised the creation of a Supreme Court of Judicature at Fort William in Calcutta. The court was established in 1774. It was a Crown court operating alongside the Company's developing system of courts. Disagreements over the respective jurisdictions of these institutions became an important administrative difficulty.

Act and institution have different dates

The Regulating Act was passed in 1773, while the Supreme Court at Calcutta was established in 1774. The Act is associated with the first Governor-General of Bengal, not the first Governor-General of India.

Pitt's India Act of 1784

The Regulating Act did not eliminate difficulties in controlling the Company from Britain. Pitt's India Act of 1784 therefore strengthened British governmental supervision by establishing a Board of Control.

The Board of Control supervised political affairs, including civil administration, military matters and territorial revenues. The Company's Court of Directors continued to conduct its commercial business and retained important administrative functions, subject to the Board's supervisory powers.

This arrangement is commonly described as dual control: the British government exercised political supervision through the Board of Control, while the Company's directors continued to operate the organisation.

What changed, and what did not

The Acts of 1773 and 1784 increased British governmental control, but neither transferred the Company's territories directly to the Crown. The Company continued to govern India under increasingly strict parliamentary supervision. Direct Crown administration came only with the Government of India Act of 1858.

The term dual control under Pitt's India Act should also be distinguished from the earlier dual government in Bengal, associated with the Company's acquisition of revenue powers in 1765. One concerned supervision of the Company from Britain; under the other, the Company held revenue authority (Diwani), while the Nawab nominally retained responsibility for police and criminal justice (Nizamat).

Prelims focus

  • 1773: Regulating Act began parliamentary control over Company government.
  • Warren Hastings: first Governor-General of Bengal.
  • The Governor-General of Bengal was assisted by a council of 4 members under the 1773 Act.
  • 1774: Supreme Court established at Calcutta.
  • 1784: Pitt's India Act established the Board of Control.
  • Trap: The Board of Control was associated with Pitt's India Act, not the Regulating Act.

[Press Information Bureau, History of Parliamentary Democracy in India, address dated 15 May 2017, paragraphs 8–9, consulted 20 November 2026; UK Parliament, House of Commons debate, Government of India, 12 February 1858, discussion of the Acts of 1773 and 1784; UK Parliament, House of Lords debate, 19 April 1869, discussion of the Board of Control; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 2, printed pp. 21–22, 2020–21 printing.]

pictures.alt: 1773 creates the Governor-General of Bengal; 1784 adds dual control from Britain while Company rule continues; direct Crown rule begins in 1858.
pictures.caption: Pitt's India Act established political supervision without immediately abolishing Company administration.

title: Regulating Act of 1773 and Pitt's India Act of 1784

body:
What the Charter Acts changed

Parliament periodically reviewed the East India Company's privileges and governing arrangements. The principal Charter Acts of 1793, 1813, 1833 and 1853 progressively reduced its commercial monopoly, strengthened central administration and altered civil-service recruitment.

The central distinction is that the Company's trading rights declined before its governing powers ended. It could therefore remain the territorial administrator of British India even after it stopped operating as a commercial enterprise.

ActCommercial positionMain administrative significance
1793Company trading monopoly retained.Charter and governing arrangements renewed for 20 years.
1813Monopoly of trade with India largely ended; tea and China trade privileges continued.Crown sovereignty over Company territories affirmed; missionaries permitted.
1833Remaining Company trade, including tea and China trade, ended.Governor-General of India and central law-making authority established.
1853Company remained a governing body, not a trading corporation.Legislative council enlarged; competitive civil-service recruitment provided for.

Charter Act of 1793: continuation

The Charter Act of 1793 continued the Company's charter for another 20 years. Its commercial monopoly was substantially retained. This Act is chiefly remembered as a continuation of the existing system rather than a major step towards ending Company trade.

The Act must not be confused with the Cornwallis Code of 1793. The Charter Act dealt with the Company's parliamentary arrangements, whereas the Cornwallis reforms reorganised important parts of judicial, revenue and police administration, especially in Bengal.

Charter Act of 1813: monopoly reduced

The Charter Act of 1813 ended the Company's exclusive right to most trade with India, allowing other British merchants to participate. The Company nevertheless retained its privileges over tea and trade with China. Thus, it is inaccurate to say that all Company commercial rights ended in 1813.

The Act also affirmed the sovereignty of the British Crown over the Company's territories and permitted Christian missionaries to enter India. The Company continued its political and administrative responsibilities.

Charter Act of 1833: centralisation and the end of Company trade

The Charter Act of 1833 ended the remaining commercial privileges of the Company. It was required to close its trading business and concentrate on administration. Its territories continued to be governed in trust for the Crown.

The Act changed the designation Governor-General of Bengal to Governor-General of India. Lord William Bentinck became the first Governor-General of India. The distinction is important: Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General of Bengal; William Bentinck was the first Governor-General of India.

Legislative authority was centralised in the Governor-General in Council. The governments of Bombay and Madras lost their separate powers to enact laws for their Presidencies. This helped create a more uniform central law-making structure across British territories.

The Act also provided for a Law Member in the Governor-General's Council. Thomas Babington Macaulay became the first Law Member. The first Indian Law Commission was constituted in 1834, with Macaulay as its chairman, to examine and recommend the consolidation and codification of laws.

An important provision was Section 87, which stated that a person should not be disqualified from Company employment solely because of religion, place of birth, descent or colour. It established a principle against specified exclusions, although it did not produce equal access to senior offices in practice.

Charter Act of 1853: legislative and recruitment changes

The Charter Act of 1853 was the last major Charter Act of Company rule. Unlike earlier renewals, it did not guarantee Company administration for another fixed period of 20 years. Parliament could determine when its governing arrangements would end.

The Governor-General's Council was expanded for legislative business by adding 6 legislative members. These additional members participated in law-making, while the Council's executive functions remained distinct. Legislative proceedings became more developed and increasingly public, but this was not the establishment of a democratically elected Indian legislature.

The Act also provided the basis for replacing patronage-based civil-service appointments with open competitive recruitment. The subsequent Macaulay Committee report of 1854 helped shape the system, and the first competitive examinations began in 1855.

Different years mark different changes

1813 reduced the trading monopoly. 1833 ended Company trade and centralised legislation. 1853 reformed legislative arrangements and recruitment. 1858 ended Company administration.

Prelims focus

  • 1793: Charter renewed for 20 years; trading monopoly continued.
  • 1813: India trade monopoly ended, except for tea and China trade.
  • 1833: remaining Company commercial business ended.
  • William Bentinck: first Governor-General of India.
  • 1833: central legislative authority, Law Member and provision for a Law Commission.
  • 1853: 6 additional legislative members and provision for competitive recruitment.
  • Trap: The first competitive civil-service examination took place in 1855, not in 1853.

[UK Parliament, East India Company and Raj 1785–1858, section Losing privileges, consulted 20 November 2026; Government of India Act 1833, original enacted text, Sections 3–4 and 87, UK legislation archive; Law Commission of India, Early Beginnings, published 2 July 2018, paragraphs on the 1833 Charter Act and First Law Commission; Press Information Bureau, History of Parliamentary Democracy in India, 15 May 2017, paragraphs 9–12; Union Public Service Commission, About Us, section Historical Perspective, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The 1833 Act centralised law-making in the Governor-General in Council; Bombay and Madras remained administrative units but lost separate legislative powers.
pictures.caption: The 1833 Act concentrated law-making authority at the all-India level.

title: Charter Acts of 1793, 1813, 1833 and 1853

body:
Why Company rule ended

The uprising of 1857 exposed serious tensions within Company rule. After the British suppressed the rebellion, Parliament decided that the East India Company should no longer exercise the government of British India.

The Government of India Act of 1858, enacted on 2 August 1858, transferred the Company's governing powers and its Indian territories to the British Crown. The central change was the replacement of a government operated by a chartered company with one conducted directly in the name of the British monarch.

New arrangements in Britain and India

Under the Act, the Secretary of State for India, a member of the British government, received the authority previously exercised through the Company's directors and the Board of Control. The Secretary of State was assisted by a Council of India consisting of 15 members, established in Britain.

In India, the Governor-General continued to head the central government, now acting as the Crown's representative and commonly styled the Viceroy. A viceroy represented the monarch in governing India, while the Governor-General remained the principal constitutional-administrative office.

Lord Canning was the last Governor-General under Company rule and the first Viceroy under Crown rule. His offices illustrate the change in the source of governmental authority rather than the creation of an entirely new system of district administration.

Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858

The transfer was formally proclaimed in India on 1 November 1858. Queen Victoria's Proclamation addressed the princes, chiefs and people of India. It announced the change of government and stated principles intended to reassure Indian subjects after the rebellion.

The Proclamation promised non-interference with religious beliefs and worship, equal protection of the law and impartial consideration for government service according to qualifications. It also accepted the continuation of treaties and engagements made with Indian princely rulers under Company authority.

These were declarations of governmental policy. They should not be treated as proof that social, judicial or administrative discrimination disappeared. British racial privilege continued to affect appointments and justice.

The end of Company rule and the legal dissolution of the Company were different events. Its administrative powers ended in 1858, whereas the Company itself was formally dissolved in 1874.

Continuity beneath the change of authority

The change to Crown rule did not immediately replace every district office, court or police arrangement. British administrators continued using and reforming institutions developed during Company rule. This continuity explains why the collector, civil service and judicial hierarchy remained central to colonial government after 1858.

Prelims focus

  • 1857: uprising against Company rule.
  • 2 August 1858: Government of India Act received royal assent.
  • 1858: administrative power transferred from the Company to the Crown.
  • Secretary of State for India: assisted by a Council of India of 15 members.
  • Lord Canning: last Company Governor-General and first Viceroy.
  • 1 November 1858: Queen Victoria's Proclamation announced Crown rule in India.
  • Trap: Crown rule began in 1858; the Company's formal dissolution occurred in 1874.

[Government of India Act 1858, original enacted text dated 2 August 1858, Sections 1–3 and 7, UK legislation archive; UK Parliament, East India Company and Raj 1785–1858, section End of Company rule, consulted 20 November 2026; British Library, archival catalogue IOR/L/PS/20/MEMO32/1, Proclamation by the Queen in Council to the Princes, Chiefs, and People of India, published at Allahabad on 1 November 1858; Cambridge University Press, The Queen's Urdu: Translating Colonial Secularity in Victoria's 1858 Proclamation, discussion of religious non-interference and access to office, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The transfer of authority was publicly announced in India in November 1858.

pictures.alt: In 1858, Crown authorities replaced Company authorities in Britain; the Governor-General continued in India as Governor-General and Viceroy. Canning was first Viceroy.
